newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Tibet's Dalai Lama arrives in Taiwan amid protests.
newsitem.headline: Tibet's Dalai Lama arrives in Taiwan amid protests.

text.p: Tibet's exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, arrived in Taiwan on Saturday for a six-day visit that has angered China despite being billed as a purely religious journey.
The Tibetan Buddhist god-king's plane touched down at the southern port city of Kaohsiung after a flight from Singapore.
Outside the airport, hundreds of Taiwan political activists wielded banners, beat drums and shouted slogans supporting or condemning the visit of the Dalai Lama.

Staking out Kaohsiung airport and separated by riot police, the opposing groups either praised the monk as a brave defender of Tibetan rights against an oppressive China, or denounced him as aiming to separate Tibet from China.

"By saying no to China, the Dalai Lama is a shining example for (Taiwan President) Lee Teng-hui," a banner carried by the Taiwan Independence Party, which advocates the island's own independence from China, said.

"Hi Mr. Lee. If you want that Nobel Prize, say no to China!" another banner read, referring to the Dalai Lama's winning the 1989 Nobel Peace Prize for his non-violent campaign for autonomy in his Himalayan homeland.
Members of Taiwan's pro-unification Labour Party accused the Dalai Lama, revered as a Buddhist god-king in Tibet, of aiming to achieve political aims under the pretence of a religious visit.
"Against Tibetan independence, for one nation and one China unity," Labour Party protesters, wearing T-shirts saying "Chinese unification", shouted at the airport.
"We support autonomy for Tibet, but we are against mixing politics and religion," a Labour Party protester said.
The Dalai Lama was scheduled to visit the Fukuangshan Temple, a principle Buddhist centre in southern Taiwan, on Saturday afternoon.
This was the Dalai Lama's first visit in Chinese territory since he and thousands of followers fled his Himalayan homeland in 1959 after the failure of an anti-Chinese uprising.

The Dalai Lama and his Taiwan hosts have insisted his visit is purely religious but communist China has attacked his journey and planned meeting with Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui as collusion between "splittists" who were struggling for the same goal -- independence from China for both Taiwan and Tibet.

Taiwan and China separated after a bitter civil war ended in 1949. Both governments still vow to seek eventual re-unification, but Taipei says unity is not possible until communist China undergoes political liberalisation.
